query: For an FCC/BCC high-entropy-alloy protective coating susceptible to progressive plastic deformation during continuous loading, what testable mechanistic hypothesis could explain its creep resistance? Specify the governing factor and rationale, an unspecified controlled comparison that would reveal it, predicted observations relative to the starting baseline, the operating boundaries under sustained stress, supporting prior evidence, and a clear falsification criterion.

generation.hypothesis: Refining the microstructural architecture of the FCC/BCC high-entropy-alloy protective coating via thermomechanical pretreatments will improve its creep resistance by establishing more effective barriers to dislocation nucleation and motion at the interface between phases.
generation.material_initial_state: An as-deposited FCC/BCC dual-phase high-entropy-alloy protective coating with a relatively coarse and unoptimized microstructure.
generation.intervention: Apply a controlled thermomechanical pretreatment designed to refine the grain structure and optimize the phase distribution (i.e., enhancing the coherency at FCC/BCC interfaces).
generation.conditions: Constant-load creep testing under elevated temperatures (e.g., 500–600°C) in the steady-state creep regime, as examined via in situ electron microscopy (TEM and EBSD).
generation.structural_mediator: A refined microstructure characterized by finer grains and enhanced interface coherency between the FCC and BCC phases, which act as more effective physical barriers.
generation.mechanism: The pretreatment-induced microstructural refinement increases the density of effective barriers that impede dislocation nucleation and slow dislocation motion during creep. This delays the accumulation of plastic deformation and retards the transition to accelerated (tertiary) creep.
generation.predicted_outcome: Compared to the as-deposited baseline, the pretreated coatings will exhibit lower steady-state creep strain rates, more stable microstructural features (fewer dislocations propagating across interfaces), and a delayed onset of tertiary creep when subjected to continuous loading at elevated temperature.
generation.baseline: The as-deposited coating, which is expected to demonstrate higher creep strain rates and more active dislocation dynamics under the same testing conditions.
generation.boundary: The improvement in creep resistance is anticipated under moderate sustained stress and temperatures between 500°C and 600°C; results may differ at extreme stress levels or temperatures beyond this range, where other deformation mechanisms might dominate.
generation.uncertainty: The exact quantitative reduction in creep rate and the relative contribution of each phase (FCC vs. BCC) in resisting creep remain uncertain until detailed in situ measurements are performed. Moreover, interactions between phase evolution and dislocation dynamics may introduce additional variability.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of protective coatings: one set in the as-deposited state and one set after subjecting them to a prescribed thermomechanical pretreatment to refine the microstructure. Perform constant-load creep tests at 500–600°C while continuously monitoring the evolution of microstructural features using in situ TEM and EBSD. Execute interrupted tests to capture the microstructural state during steady-state creep.
measurements: Creep strain rate over time (from LVDT or equivalent displacement sensors)
Dislocation density and propagation via TEM imaging
Grain size and phase interface quality via EBSD analysis
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If pretreated coatings do not exhibit a statistically significant lower steady-state creep strain rate and a reduced progression of dislocation activity compared to the as-deposited coatings under identical load and temperature conditions, then the hypothesis that microstructural refinement enhances creep resistance is falsified.

cited_evidence.text: A clear transition in creep mechanisms is observed, evolving from diffusion-dominated deformation at low stresses to dislocation nucleation, glide, and interaction at intermediate conditions, and ultimately to stress-induced phase transformation at higher stresses and temperatures. This progression is corroborated by atomic-scale structural evolution and steady-state creep theory. Under identical conditions, HESAs show markedly superior creep resistance to HEAs, mainly due to the strong blocking effect of γ/γ′ interfaces on dislocation motion and atomic transport. Both the γ/γ′ lattice misfit and γ′ volume fraction exert a critical influence on creep resistance. The relationship between misfit magnitude and creep behavior is non-monotonic: moderate negative misfit enhances interfacial coherency and stabilizes the microstructure, thereby improving creep resistance, whereas excessively large misfit increases interfacial strain energy and deteriorates performance. A negative misfit is generally more effective in resisting creep because it strengthens the γ/γ′ interface and reduces dislocation transmissibility. In addition, increasing the γ′ volume fraction significantly enhances creep

In the present study, the tensile creep tests under constant stress were performed on multiple fine-grained CoCrFeNiMn HEA specimens in the temperature range of 500–600 °C. Specifically, some tests were interrupted at the steady-state stages and cooled quickly to reserve the crept microstructures for examining the microstructural evolution. The objective was to reveal the inherent relationship between microstructural evolution and creep properties of single-phase CoCrFeNiMn high-entropy alloy.
